Welcome to the English marathon for police officers! 👮

The marathon has five parts:

Do everything as slowly as you need! Good luck! 🍀 Remember, your teachers are here to help you if you need them. 🙂

Part 1: Introduction

Get tips on how to learn vocabulary by yourself.

It’s a good idea to have a routine when you learn vocabulary. [routine — something you do often and usually in the same way]

For example:

  • a weekly routine when you study a set of words and phrases from the marathon for at least [not less than] 30–45 minutes;
  • a daily [happening every day] routine when you revise that unit [study it again]. You may only need to revise for five or ten minutes each time.
  • After you’ve started the course, it should be enough to have 2 group lessons and revise new vocabulary and grammar for 5–10 minutes every day. You may want to have one day off, with no English at all.
  • If there’s something interesting to listen to or read at your level, it will work perfectly well. For example, a podcast for your level or small blog articles. Most importantly, you must enjoy it!

Self-study tips

When you are studying words on your own [without help of anyone else] for the first time, you need to be active when you are learning.

  • With a new word or phrase, say it aloud [speak it so you can hear it], and repeat it to yourself silently [in your head, not speaking]. Remember to check the pronunciation of new words because it’s hard to fix wrong pronunciation later :)
  • It’s a good idea to write new words in your notebook or keep them in one document on the laptop or phone.
  • Always try to write an example sentence for new words. You can choose an example from a dictionary, but an example from your own life will often help you to remember a word because it activates emotional memory, e.g. I shared a flat with a German boy when I had my 4th semester and this helped me improve colloquial German.

Revising words

  • When you are revising words or a lesson one or two days later, it is also important to be as active as possible.
  • Test yourself, e.g. look at a word and cover the meaning. Can you remember what the meaning is? If you can’t, check the meaning, then come back to the word in five minutes’ time and test yourself again.
  • Look at what you wrote in your notebook or digital document when you first studied the unit. Is there any new information you want to add, e.g. something about the pronunciation, or a common word partner?

Expanding your vocabulary [making sth bigger]

When you learn a new word, you may want to find antonyms or related parts of speech. Synonyms might be useful as well. For example, if you learnt increase, you might look for the opposite decrease. If you learned a noun choice, you might benefit from learning the verb choose.

Answer the questions

  1. Do you revise vocabulary that you study? If so, how often?
  2. Have you ever looked for synonyms, antonyms or related parts of speech?

Courts and punishment

Reading: a short story

The Cheap Ticket

Anna wanted to save money, so on Sunday she took the bus home instead of a taxi. The bus stopped in every village, but she wasn’t in a hurry. She sat by the window, listened to music and watched people get on and off.

She paid by card at the front. The machine made a strange noise, but she didn’t worry. Half an hour later, a ticket inspector got on. “Tickets, please!” Anna smiled calmly and gave her phone to be scanned. The inspector frowned. “I’m sorry, there’s no payment here.”

“But I paid! There must be a mistake!” said Anna. It was no use. She was caught without a valid ticket. It was only a minor offence, but she still had to pay a fine of 800 hryvnias. She felt completely innocent: the machine made the mistake, not her.

That evening she told her brother. He laughed. “Next they’ll take you to court. You’ll be found guilty, and they’ll send you to prison!”

“Very funny,” Anna said. She was not in the mood for jokes. “Why was I punished for a machine’s mistake?” The bus ticket and the fine cost 900 hryvnias. A taxi cost only 300.

Exercise 1. Listen to the audio

Real Easy English: talking about work

Show the transcript

Georgie: Hello and welcome to Real Easy English, where we have real conversations in easy English to help you learn. I'm Georgie.

Becca: And I'm Becca. You can find a video version of this podcast on our website and test yourself with a worksheet on bbclearningenglish.com.

Georgie: Hello Becca. How are you?

Becca: I'm really well, thank you, Georgie. How about yourself?

Georgie: Yes, I'm good, thank you. Are you having a busy week?

Becca: It has been a little bit busy, but also quite fun. How about yours?

Georgie: Me too. I've had a busy week, but it's going well. And Becca, today we're talking about work. We're going to talk about what we're good at, at work, and also what we do when things go wrong.

Becca: Ooh. OK.

Georgie: So, what do you like about work?

Becca: I like that we have different tasks to do in the day, and some of them are creative, and then other tasks you really need to, kind of, put more thought and focus into.

Georgie: Becca, do you ever find work stressful?

Becca: Of course. I think that you will find work stressful at some point during your job or your career. Yeah, I think if I haven't planned things well – if I haven't done the preparation well – then I find things a bit stressful.

Georgie: Yeah.

Becca: How about yourself?

Georgie: Yeah, me too. When we have lots of projects as well, I feel like when we have a lot of things going on, it can be stressful to, kind of, juggle different tasks. And when we need to publish a new podcast or a new video series, it can be... there can be a lot of pressure to get things done.

Becca: So, would you say that you're someone who gets stressed easily at work? Because you seem to be quite calm all the time.

Georgie: Yeah. No, I don't actually get too stressed very often. Even when there's a bit of pressure at work, I tend to stay quite calm. I always just think, there's no point in worrying. Becca: Yeah, as I previously mentioned, I think if... I'm usually quite an organised person but, you know, there are some times where I feel a bit disorganised. Georgie: Yeah.

Becca: Not just in work, but in my general life.

Georgie: So, you get nervous if you're not feeling organised. But are you good at being organised?

Becca: Yes. If I write things down, then I tend to stay organised. It's likely that I won't feel very stressed. I can start to relax a bit when I know that, you know, I've ticked things off my list. Do you write to-do lists?

Georgie: I do. I do write to-do lists. And that can be really helpful to, kind of, keep calm because you have your whole plan on a page that you can see. And you can, kind of, know where you are in your week, which is really helpful.

Becca: Yeah.

Georgie: What happens when things go wrong at work? What... how do you, kind of... how do you deal with these situations?

Part 4: In the office

Learn office vocabulary and practise giving your opinion.

Cabinet or office?

Cabinet

Cabinet — a piece of furniture with doors and shelves or drawers, used for storing or showing things.
Filing cabinet — a piece of office furniture.

Example: He took the papers from the top drawer of the filing cabinet.

Office

Office — a room where someone has a desk and works, on their own or with other people; a building that belongs to a company or an organization, with rooms where people can work at desks.

Example: Sorry, Ann’s not in her office right now. Dan shares an office with Lisa. Mark is OOO (= out of office) until Monday.

Note: Ukrainian learners often confuse cabinet and office.
Example: Ann is not in her cabinet now. Ann is not in her office right now.

Office work

I work as an administrative assistant at a police station. My job involves1 a lot of different tasks. Every morning I organise2 the duty sergeant’s schedule and make appointments3 with witnesses and lawyers. I also arrange4 transport for officers who need to go to court. Twice a week I attend meetings5 with the chief and write down what was decided.

Today has been a difficult day. The photocopier has broken down6, so I can’t copy the case files. Also, my computer isn’t working7, and the printer has run out of paper8, so I can’t print the witness statements either. I have loads of work to do9, and the deadline is at five o’clock!

Giving your opinion

Read the dialogue and study the phrases.

Mark: Anna, what do you think of our new body cameras?

Anna: Personally, I think they’re very useful. They protect both officers and the public.

Mark: I totally agree with you. They are also good evidence in court.

Anna: And what do you think about using more technology in police work?

Mark: Personally, I feel it makes our job safer, but I’m worried about people’s privacy.

Anna: I partly agree with you. Privacy is important, but criminals use technology too, so we need it.

Mark: That’s true. Some people say officers don’t need cameras at all.

Anna: I disagree completely! Cameras give us clear evidence and protect us from false complaints.

Asking for someone’s opinion

  1. What do you think of …? (specific)
  2. What do you think about …? (general)

Introducing your own opinion

  1. Personally, I think…
  2. Personally, I feel…

Agreeing and disagreeing with someone

  1. I totally agree with you. – Я цілком з тобою погоджуюся.
  2. I partly agree with you. – Я частково погоджуюся.
  3. I disagree completely. – Я цілком не згодний.
